cards.body: Read the company's website, check their recent posts, and re-read the job posting so you know exactly what they need. Then prepare two or three questions to ask them — 'What's a typical day like here?' works everywhere from coffee shops to IT desks.
cards.title: Research beats winging it

cards.body: Prepare three short stories from your life: a time you helped someone, a time you solved a problem, a time you worked on a team. School projects, volunteering, even helping family all count — interviewers remember stories, not adjectives.
cards.title: Build your three stories

cards.body: You walk in ten minutes early with two printed resumes, a pen, your ID, and a list of two references with phone numbers. The interviewer hasn't printed anything — you just saved the conversation. Preparation reads as professionalism.

Dress one notch above the job's uniform: collared shirt for retail, neat and clean for food service. And eat something beforehand — a rumbling stomach in a quiet interview room is a distraction you can prevent.

choices: What they do, what the role involves, and a few questions to ask
cards.explain: Knowing the company lets you connect your experience to their needs, and having questions ready shows genuine interest instead of desperation.
cards.q: What should you know before walking into any interview?

choices: 'What's the schedule like, and what does training look like?'
questions.explain: Questions about the actual work show you picture yourself doing the job. Save pay and promotion talk for after they want you.
questions.q: Best question to ask a retail interviewer?

choices: Exactly on time to the second
questions.explain: Ten minutes shows eagerness without hovering. Much earlier and you become an awkward lobby fixture.
questions.q: When should you arrive for an interview?

choices: Anything real: school, volunteering, helping family, part-time gigs
questions.explain: Experience is experience. Interviewers care what you did and learned, not whether someone paid you for it.
questions.q: You have no formal job history. What counts as experience?

choices: Printed resumes, ID, references, a pen
questions.explain: Bringing your own copies signals preparation and saves the day when theirs aren't handy. The pen is for any forms.
questions.q: What should you physically bring to an interview?

choices: Something specific about them — a product, value, or recent news
'It was the first posting I saw'
questions.explain: 'Why us?' tests whether you care about this job or just any job. One specific detail beats ten generic compliments.
questions.q: When they ask 'Why do you want to work here?', the winning answer mentions…

flashcards.back: Research the company, prepare stories and questions, bring resumes/ID/references, arrive ten minutes early.
Ask about the work itself — schedule, training, team, typical day. Shows you picture yourself in the role.
School projects, volunteering, family responsibilities, part-time gigs. What you did and learned matters.
One notch above the job's uniform. Clean, neat, simple.

cards.body: STAR stands for Situation, Task, Action, Result. Describe the setup in one line, say what you had to do, spend most of your time on what you actually did, and end with the outcome. Sixty to ninety seconds total — it's a story, not a documentary.
cards.title: STAR: the answer formula

cards.body: Present, past, future — in that order. 'I'm a second-year game design student working part-time in food service (present). I've handled rush shifts and trained two new hires (past). I'm looking for a role where I can keep building customer skills while I finish school (future).' Sixty seconds, job-relevant, done.
cards.title: 'Tell me about yourself' in 60 seconds

cards.body: Interviewer: 'What's your biggest weakness?' You: 'I used to get flustered when plans changed mid-shift. Now I keep a quick reset routine — pause, reprioritize, communicate. My last manager actually complimented how I handled a double-booking.' Real weakness, concrete fix, evidence.

Never badmouth a past boss, teacher, or workplace — it makes interviewers imagine you talking about them next. If a job was rough, frame it forward: 'I learned I do my best work in busier, team-based environments.'

cards.explain: Interviewers are hiring you for what you'll do. Situation sets the scene in one line; the Action is the audition.
cards.q: In a STAR answer, which part deserves the most time?

questions.explain: STAR turns rambling anecdotes into tight, convincing stories: setup, your job, your actions, the payoff.

choices: Present situation, relevant past, why this role next
questions.explain: They're asking 'why should we hire you,' not 'tell me your biography.' Keep it current, relevant, and under a minute.
questions.q: Best structure for 'Tell me about yourself'?

choices: Name a real one and explain how you're improving it
questions.explain: Everyone has weaknesses; claiming none signals zero self-awareness. A real one plus a fix shows growth.

choices: Redirect to what you learned and what you want next
questions.explain: Badmouthing poisons the room — they picture themselves as your next complaint. Forward-looking framing keeps you hireable.
questions.q: Asked why you left a bad job, you should…

choices: Something specific you noticed plus a real question
questions.explain: One thoughtful question ('I saw you just expanded weekend hours — how's the team handling it?') proves you did homework. Silence suggests you don't care.
questions.q: 'Do you have questions for us?' — best move?

flashcards.back: Situation, Task, Action, Result. One line of setup, most time on Action, end with the outcome. 60–90 seconds.
Present, past, future — job-relevant, sixty seconds. Not your life story.
Name a genuine one and show concrete steps you're taking to improve it. Never a humble-brag.
It makes them imagine you complaining about them next. Frame the past forward: what you learned, what you want.

cards.body: Send a short thank-you within 24 hours: thank them for their time, mention one specific thing you discussed, restate your interest. Three sentences beat three paragraphs — and most candidates skip this entirely, so it makes you memorable.
cards.title: The 24-hour thank-you note

cards.body: No timeline given? Wait about a week, then send one polite follow-up: 'Just checking in — still very interested in the role.' One nudge shows enthusiasm; three makes you the story they tell at lunch. Never follow up the same day.
cards.title: Follow up once, not five times

cards.body: You get two part-time offers: Shop A pays $1 more per hour but schedules you randomly, including during your classes. Shop B pays slightly less but guarantees your class schedule and is a ten-minute walk away. For a student, B is the better-paying job once you count the real costs.

You can negotiate politely even for hourly work: 'Is there any flexibility on the starting rate? I bring six months of cashier experience and weekend availability.' Ask once, accept gracefully. The bigger student win is often scheduling, not cents.

choices: Schedule fit, commute, and total real costs — not just the hourly number
cards.explain: A higher rate means nothing if shifts clash with classes or the commute eats an hour unpaid. Evaluate the whole package.
cards.q: Comparing two part-time offers as a student, what matters most?

questions.explain: Fast, short, specific. It keeps you fresh in their mind while they're still deciding.
questions.q: When should the thank-you note go out?

choices: Thank them, name one specific topic, restate interest — briefly
A five-paragraph essay on your life
questions.explain: Specificity proves you were engaged; brevity respects their inbox. Generic notes get generic responses.
questions.q: What goes in a good thank-you note?

choices: One polite check-in after about a week
A message every hour on day one
questions.explain: Hiring takes time. One nudge signals interest; repeated contact signals you'll be exhausting to manage.
questions.q: No word after the interview and no timeline was given. You should…

choices: 'Is there flexibility on the starting rate, given my experience?'
questions.explain: Polite, specific, one ask. Many hourly roles have a small range — and asking costs nothing when done respectfully.
questions.q: Most professional way to negotiate a part-time offer?

choices: Get the key details in writing before deciding
Decide by gut feeling in the room
questions.explain: Start date, rate, hours, schedule — confirmed in writing. Verbal promises evaporate; written ones protect both sides.
questions.q: Before accepting any offer, you should…

flashcards.back: Within 24 hours. Three sentences: thanks, one specific detail from the chat, restated interest.
One polite message after about a week if no timeline was given. Never the same day.
Hourly rate plus schedule fit, commute, and flexibility around classes. The whole package, not one number.
Ask once, politely, with a reason ('my experience', 'weekend availability'). Accept gracefully either way.
